Series::unflatten¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::unflatten(
    std::int64_t dim,
    pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int sizes) const

Expanding One Axis Into Several Axes¶

unflatten() replaces one receiver axis with a sequence of axes whose product equals the original extent. Values retain their row-major order; only their coordinates change. It is the precise inverse of flattening the same adjacent axes when no intervening permutation has changed their order.

If the receiver has shape [2,12], then unflatten(1,{3,4}) produces [2,3,4]. All axes before dim remain before the inserted axes, and all axes after dim remain after them. Negative dim values are normalized from the back, so -1 selects the final axis.

sizes must be nonempty. Its extents must be non-negative, except that exactly one -1 may request inference from the selected receiver extent and the other specified extents. The inferred extent must be integral and unambiguous. In particular, {2,-1} can split an empty extent into {2,0}, whereas {0,-1} is rejected because every inferred value would have product zero. Product overflow is rejected before shape construction.

Storage, Metadata, And Reverse Mode¶

The output preserves dtype and platform. When the receiver’s storage layout can represent the expanded axes directly, unflatten() returns a metadata view rather than copying values; otherwise the reshape machinery materializes the required layout. The receiver is never mutated.

Reverse mode collapses the inserted axes back into the original extent. Every output coordinate maps to exactly one input coordinate, so no sensitivity is summed merely because the rank changed.

Examples¶

1. Split an axis with explicit extents¶

const auto flat = pluss::series::arange(
    0.0, 24.0, 1.0, pluss::ScalarType::Float64).reshape({2, 12});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, flat.unflatten(1, {3, 4}));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3,4], strides=[12,4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=24, contiguous=true)
data[0, :, :] =
⎡ 0.0000 1.0000  2.0000  3.0000 ⎤
⎢ 4.0000 5.0000  6.0000  7.0000 ⎥
⎣ 8.0000 9.0000 10.0000 11.0000 ⎦

data[1, :, :] =
⎡ 12.0000 13.0000 14.0000 15.0000 ⎤
⎢ 16.0000 17.0000 18.0000 19.0000 ⎥
⎣ 20.0000 21.0000 22.0000 23.0000 ⎦

The original final coordinate j becomes coordinates {j / 4, j % 4}.

2. Infer one extent and use a negative axis¶

const auto expanded = flat.unflatten(-1, {2, -1});
std::cout << "shape=" << expanded.sizes() << '\n';

Output¶

shape=[2, 2, 6]

The selected extent is twelve. After fixing the first inserted extent at two, the inferred extent is six.

3. Infer a zero extent without ambiguity¶

const auto empty =
    pluss::series::empty({0}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64)
        .unflatten(0, {2, -1});
std::cout << "shape=" << empty.sizes() << '\n';

Output¶

shape=[2, 0]

The known nonzero factor makes the inferred zero unique. By contrast, {0,-1} is ambiguous and throws.

4. Differentiate through the shape view¶

auto tracked = flat.clone();
tracked.tracks_slope_(true);
tracked.unflatten(1, {3, 4}).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, tracked.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,12], strides=[12,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=24, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000 ... 1.0000 ⎤
⎣ 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000 ... 1.0000 ⎦

5. Reject a non-factorable request¶

try {
  (void)flat.unflatten(1, {5, -1});
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

unflatten: sizes do not multiply to the selected dimension

Multiple inferred extents, an empty sizes list, dimensions below -1, an out-of-range axis, and overflowing products are also rejected.

See Also¶

  • flatten() combines adjacent axes.

  • reshape() specifies the complete destination shape.

  • view() requests a compatible metadata view.
